newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new leftist government drafting wish-list.
newsitem.headline: France's new leftist government drafting wish-list.

text.p: France's new leftist government, fresh from its first cabinet meeting with conservative President Jacques Chirac, has begun compiling a list of urgent tasks and priorities for Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, a spokeswoman said.
"The prime minister will make a declaration of general policy and announce his calendar and priorities in a few days," government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said.

"At the present time, the various members of the government are drafting lists of urgent tasks and at the same time lists of what should be proposed to the prime minister as new priorities. So this matter is going forward progressively," she added.

Jospin, on his first official international trip, chatted briefly with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair about the difficulties facing the European Union's plans for European monetary union, according to a British official.
"They both spoke of the difficulties the single currency would face," the official said without offering details.
Jospin and Blair were in Malmo, Sweden, attending a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties.
Jospin was to address the conference and hold more talks with Blair later on Friday.
France's new leftist cabinet fanned out across Paris on Thursday to take over their respective ministries in a series of ceremonies marking the formal transition of power.
The 26-strong cabinet, announced on Wednesday night, includes several women in senior posts, Communists for the first time since 1984, and a Green minister of the environment.
A leftist alliance including Socialists, Communists and Greens swept into power last Sunday in an upset parliamentary election victory over the previous centre-right majority.
After just one day on the job, "our team is ready to work, drawn together, motivated, enthusiastic," Trautmann said.
The buoyuant new cabinet members had gathered at the Elysee presidential palace on Thursday morning for an initial meeting with a grim-faced President Chirac.
"Here we are in a new period of 'cohabitation'," Chirac said, using the French term for power-sharing between a government and president of different political persuasions.
It is the third era of cohabitation in the history of France's Fifth Republic, which began in 1958, but the first between a left-wing prime minister and a right-wing head of state.

Jospin, who led the left's upset victory over Chirac's centre-right allies in Sunday's National Assembly election, said the 30-minute cabinet talks launching power-sharing went "well, very well". He said the tone was serious but relaxed.

After reacting negatively to the prospect of a leftist government during the campaign, the Paris Bourse saluted the broadly pro-European government, in which Communists hostile to a European single currency were confined to the transport and sports ministries.
The CAC-40 stock index gained 2.11 percent for the day.
New Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou said her first and most urgent task would be to restore citizens' confidence in the independence of the judicial system.

Judges have opened several investigations into politically charged cases this week, including illicit party funding, alleged rigged public tenders and illegal bugging, which had been on ice until after Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

Chirac's disastrous gamble in calling parliamentary elections 10 months ahead of schedule, only to lose the centre-right's huge majority in parliament, has left his Gaullist RPR party in deep disarray.

Former parliament speaker Philippe Seguin, who led the 1992 campaign against the Maastricht treaty in France, formally announced his candidacy to succeed defeated prime minister Alain Juppe as RPR leader.
Senior Gaullist Charles Pasqua, a Seguin supporter, said there was broad consensus for a special party congress on July 5, at which time a new leader would be chosen.
